co_central_ridgeline_including_ship_s_pr.blurb: A small boulder cluster on the ridgetop at Rotary Park, on the west side of Fort Collins near Horsetooth Reservoir. Nineteen problems run along a low ridgeline, and the great majority are V2 or easier, so it suits beginners and warm-ups, with a few problems reaching about V5. The standout is Ship's Prow, a distinctive blocky formation with a heavily chalked crack, where eight or nine lines can be strung together. The ridge faces west, and with so many separate boulders you can usually find sun or shade to suit the day. Climbing here is possible through most of the year.

co_millenium_boulder_the.blurb: A big square block sitting on its own in the meadow of Matthews-Winters Park, just northwest of Morrison on the Denver side of the foothills. This is a hard boulder: of the nineteen problems, roughly half are V6 or harder and a handful reach V9 and V10, with a few friendlier lines in the V1 to V5 range. Landings are flat, which makes it a comfortable place to work difficult moves. The walk from the trailhead is easy, around ten to fifteen minutes. Warm-season visitors should watch for rattlesnakes around and beneath the block.

co_headstone_the.blurb: One of the signature walls at Devil's Head in the South Platte region of the Colorado foothills. It is a tall yellow face, about 250 feet, that looks west and picks up sun from midday until evening. The nineteen routes here mix twelve sport lines with seven trad lines, running from 5.8 up to the low 5.13s, with the bulk falling between 5.9 and 5.11. Several climbs are two or three pitches. The wall is reached on foot from the Zinn Overlook area, by a faint trail that drops across a small talus field to the base. It is widely treated as a must-do when visiting Devil's Head.

co_installation_wall.blurb: The first wall you meet at The Gallery, a bolted and trad cragging area above Old Stage Road in the hills outside Colorado Springs. The wall holds nineteen routes, mostly sport (fifteen) with a few trad lines, from easy 5.6 climbing up to 5.12. Its sweet spot is 5.10, where eight of the routes land, so it suits climbers working the middle grades. Rock on this stretch is mostly vertical to overhanging and is said to be better than at the nearby Hurricane Ridge. The walk from the roadside pullout is short, and some holds may still be loose.

co_mushroom_massif.blurb: A broad, striking crag on the south side of the South Fork of St. Vrain Canyon, near Lyons, with its base well above the river. Mostly trad, it has nineteen routes, sixteen of them on gear and three bolted, from 5.8 through 5.12, with most between 5.8 and 5.10. The rock is grainy and rounded, and this is a crack-climbing canyon. Most climbs face north and remain shady even in midsummer, which makes it a good escape from hot days. The approach involves crossing the river, which can mean wading in spring and early summer, and the slope has plenty of poison ivy.

co_officer_s_gulch_west.blurb: A compact sport crag in 10 Mile Canyon, the stretch of I-70 between Frisco and Copper Mountain, at roughly 9,900 feet. The wall sits above the north side of the highway; you can hear traffic, though it feels fairly sheltered. Nineteen mostly single-pitch routes cover easy to moderate ground: nearly all fall between about 5.7 and 5.10, with one top-rope-only line near 5.11. Climbs are roughly 40 to 80 feet tall. The wall looks mostly northeast, getting sun from morning into early afternoon in high season. A cairned path of about ten minutes leads in. Many lines are recent, so test holds before trusting them.
